clue.text: Food for Neddy the Greek

parts.note: GR is the standard abbreviation for Greek
Neddy is a traditional British pet name for a donkey, so an ass

explanation.surface: What does one feed a donkey belonging to a Greek?
explanation.walkthrough: The clue order is Neddy then Greek, but the answer puts GR first. 'Food for Neddy' also reads as a whole phrase, which neatly suits the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Grazing animals eat it, so it is fodder or food for livestock.

clue.text: Arm Colditz type with the German explosive

parts.note: a gun is a firearm, an arm
Colditz Castle was a German camp for prisoners of war, so its inmates were POWs
der is a German word for the

explanation.surface: Supplying a prisoner of war and a German with something to blow things up.
explanation.walkthrough: Colditz was a castle in Saxony used as a Second World War camp for Allied officers who were prisoners of war (POW).
explanation.definitionFit: The black powder mixture of saltpetre, sulphur and charcoal is the original explosive.

clue.text: National winner ended with vulgar speech.

indicators.note: only the ending of the horse's name is kept, so its front is dropped

parts.note: L'Escargot won the Grand National steeplechase in 1975

explanation.surface: A racing champion finished up shouting coarse language.
explanation.walkthrough: The Grand National is Britain's famous steeplechase at Aintree. Its 1975 winner L'Escargot ends in the answer, so drop LESC.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang or the jargon of a group, low or vulgar speech, is called this.

clue.text: Ain't nurse terribly gloomy ?

indicators.note: terribly suggests something badly done, so these letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: Is the nurse awfully depressed?
explanation.walkthrough: 'terribly' rearranges AIN'T NURSE.
explanation.definitionFit: Born under Saturn in astrology meant having a sullen, dark, morose temperament.

clue.text: Lane's BBC line

parts.note: the word wanted goes in front of both Lane (a famous London street market) and Line (a long-running BBC radio panel show of women)

explanation.surface: A broadcaster's catchphrase belonging to someone called Lane.
explanation.walkthrough: Petticoat Lane is a Sunday street market in East London; Petticoat Line was a BBC radio panel game of the 1960s and 70s with an all-woman panel. One word completes both names.
explanation.definitionFit: The underskirt word is the shared first half of a London market's name and of a BBC radio programme's title.

clue.text: Fuel here Margaret, about a half-bottle anyway

indicators.note: about means going round, so one piece surrounds the others

parts.note: Peg is a pet form of Margaret

indicators.note: anyway, as any way, means the letters can go in any order
half means only the first three of the six letters of bottle are used

explanation.surface: Margaret, collect your fuel, with roughly half a bottle at any rate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'anyway' (read as 'any way') rearranges the half-bottle's letters to TBO; 'half-bottle' suggests a drink, but only half the word is used. Peat is a turf fuel dug from wet moorland.
explanation.definitionFit: Turf is cut from a wet moorland site and burnt as fuel, so the bog is where that comes from.

clue.text: More indisposed in a way to erect a lattice

indicators.note: to erect is to raise up, and in a down entry this turns the letters upwards so they read from bottom to top
in places the sicker word inside the street

parts.note: ST is short for street, a way
iller means sicker, more indisposed

explanation.surface: Sicker, the gardener puts up a framework anyway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to erect' reverses the whole of SILLERT, since in a down entry raising letters means reading them upwards. 'way' is ST, short for street.
explanation.definitionFit: A wooden framework of crossed strips for climbing plants is a garden lattice.

clue.text: The cove admitted transposing words

indicators.note: the two words of the phrase swap places, putting the second first

parts.note: let in means admitted

explanation.surface: The chap confessed to swapping words around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cove' looks like old slang for a fellow, matching 'admitted' as confessing; it is a small bay. Swap LET IN round.
explanation.definitionFit: A small bay or narrow arm of the sea is a cove.

clue.text: Old boy, one given notice, and taking it

parts.note: OB is the abbreviation for old boy, a former pupil
a domestic servant was the classic employee given notice

explanation.surface: A former pupil, sacked, takes it on the chin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking it' means taking notice, picking up the 'notice' of the previous phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone attentive and quick to notice things is alert to the world.

clue.text: Some pretty rollicking times in Austria.

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Some very jolly holidays to be had in Austria.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' picks letters spanning 'pretty' and 'rollicking'.
explanation.definitionFit: An Alpine region of western Austria is famous for its ski resorts and lively holidays.

clue.text: A note I get to convert into cash

indicators.note: to convert something is to change its form, so these letters are changed into a new order

explanation.surface: A banknote that one is going to change for money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to convert' does double service in the surface, appearing to belong to the definition; strictly it rearranges A NOTE I GET, and 'into cash' is what is left to define the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To negotiate a bill or cheque is the banking term for turning it into money by transfer or sale.

clue.text: Beam sent out by a lotus-eater, say ?

indicators.note: say tells us the word is to be spoken, giving a match in sound only

parts.note: a lotus-eater idles away the time, so is one who lazes, a lazer

explanation.surface: A ray of light emitted by a dreamy idler.
explanation.walkthrough: The lotus-eaters of Homer's Odyssey drift in idle content; such a person 'lazes', so is a 'lazer', which sounds just like the beam.
explanation.definitionFit: A concentrated ray of coherent light is a beam produced by this device.

clue.text: Extra magpie shot

definitions.meaning: extra in its sense of outside or beyond, as in the prefix extra-
in target shooting a magpie is a hit near the edge of the target, close to the outermost ring

explanation.surface: A bonus round shooting at a black-and-white bird.
explanation.walkthrough: In rifle shooting on a ringed target, hits are named bull, inner, magpie and then the outermost ring's shot; the clue loosely equates the magpie with the edge hit.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means exterior or beyond, and also names a hit on the outermost ring of a shooting target.

clue.text: Account includes a rate revision for two parties

indicators.note: includes means one piece takes another inside it

parts.note: a bill is an account of money owed

indicators.note: a revision changes and reworks, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An invoice taking in a changed tariff agreed between two sides.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revision' rearranges A RATE to ATERA; 'Account' looks like the subject of the surface but simply gives the outer word.
explanation.definitionFit: A treaty or agreement involving two sides is two-sided, which is the meaning of the term.

clue.text: Grace-not the doctor except to his wife ?

definitions.text: Grace-not the doctor except to his wife ?

parts.words: Grace-not the doctor except to his wife ?
parts.note: two famous Graces: not W. G. Grace the cricketing doctor, but the lighthouse heroine, whose surname is also what a husband might call his wife

explanation.surface: A Grace who was no physician, unless you count what he called his spouse.
explanation.walkthrough: W. G. Grace, the great Victorian cricketer, was a qualified doctor. Grace Darling was the lighthouse keeper's daughter who rescued shipwrecked sailors in 1838; the doctor would call his wife 'darling'.
explanation.definitionFit: A heroine's surname which doubles as a term of endearment a husband uses for his spouse.

clue.text: Keepers, or, aged butlers perhaps?

definitions.meaning: keepers in the sense of things that hold or keep, such as fees or devices
old family servants such as long-serving butlers are called 'old ...'

explanation.surface: Gamekeepers, or perhaps elderly manservants?
explanation.definitionFit: Devices or fees that hold something in place, and long-serving household servants such as old butlers.

clue.text: But kept unholy by witches

parts.note: a weekly holy day of rest is to be kept holy, yet witches hold a gathering of the same name

explanation.surface: Something normally observed piously that witches celebrate wickedly instead.
explanation.walkthrough: The commandment says to keep the day of rest holy; a witches' midnight gathering is also called by that name, so they keep it 'unholy'.
explanation.definitionFit: The weekly holy day of rest shares its name with a midnight assembly of witches.

clue.text: Judges note surveyor's point of reference

parts.note: the bench is the collective term for judges
to mark is to note

explanation.surface: Magistrates take note of a surveyor's reference point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Judges note' reads as a verb phrase; in the parse 'Judges' is a noun (the bench).
explanation.definitionFit: A surveyor's mark cut into stone is a fixed height from which levels are measured.

clue.text: Its ponds aroused Pickwick's speculations

parts.note: in Dickens's Pickwick Papers, Mr Pickwick writes a paper speculating on the source of ponds in a north London district

explanation.surface: Ponds that set Mr Pickwick wondering.
explanation.walkthrough: The Pickwick Papers opens with Mr Pickwick's paper 'Speculations on the Source of the Hampstead Ponds'. The district is in north London, famous for its heath and bathing ponds.
explanation.definitionFit: A north London district whose ponds were the subject of a learned paper in Dickens.

clue.text: Bugle-call for engineers' annual outing?

parts.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, the British Army's engineering corps
a works treat was an annual outing given to employees

explanation.surface: Is a trumpet signal sounded for the army engineers' yearly day out?
explanation.walkthrough: The held clue drops 'engineers'' which the printed page shows. RE (Royal Engineers) is a common crossword abbreviation; a 'treat' was a firm's annual excursion for staff.
explanation.definitionFit: The military signal sounded at sunset, or to order withdrawal, is a bugle call.

clue.text: Headmaster's study or solarium ?

parts.note: both are places where hides get worked over: a pupil gets a caning in the head's study, and sunbathers brown their skins in a solarium

explanation.surface: Which room: the head's office or a sun lounge?
explanation.walkthrough: To 'tan someone's hide' is old British slang for a beating, once dealt out by headmasters; a solarium gives you a suntan.
explanation.definitionFit: A works where hides are cured into leather, punning on caning and suntanning.

clue.text: Can't possibly include it in : .the total study

indicators.note: include means the total takes the other letters inside it

parts.note: a sum is a total

indicators.note: possibly signals the letters may be arranged another way

explanation.surface: It cannot be counted in the overall study.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' rearranges the letters of Can't to ANCT; 'study' looks like part of the total but is the definition, a private room. 'it in' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: A private room for study or retreat, a den, is this inner holy place.

clue.text: In a telephone system Liszt appears like Marat at the end

indicators.note: In places the cleric inside the telephone system

parts.note: STD, subscriber trunk dialling, was the British system for dialling long-distance calls direct
Franz Liszt took minor orders late in life and was known as Abbé Liszt

explanation.surface: The composer turns up on a phone network, ending like a French revolutionary.
explanation.walkthrough: Jean-Paul Marat, French revolutionary, was stabbed in his bath by Charlotte Corday in 1793.
explanation.definitionFit: The revolutionary was killed with a knife, so finished up knifed in his bath.

clue.text: She was once seen on a detail, we hear

definitions.text: She was once seen on a detail, we hear

parts.words: She was once seen on a detail, we hear
parts.note: the figure who appeared on the tails side of old British pennies; 'a detail' heard aloud is 'a tail'

explanation.surface: A woman glimpsed in some fine point, so they say.
explanation.walkthrough: The seated figure with trident and shield was on the reverse (tails) of the old British penny. 'a detail' spoken sounds like 'a tail'.
explanation.definitionFit: The female personification of Britain, long shown on the reverse of coins.

clue.text: Vulgar money, not man's sole life support

definitions.meaning: slang for cash, as in dough
the Bible says man shall not live by this alone

explanation.surface: Coarse cash isn't the only thing keeping a man alive.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for money, and the staple food of the scriptural saying that man does not live by it alone.

clue.text: Spirit taken from pine

parts.note: in The Tempest, Prospero frees a sprite whom the witch Sycorax had imprisoned in a cloven pine

explanation.surface: Something alcoholic distilled from pine trees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirit' suggests turpentine or a liquor distilled from pine; it is Shakespeare's sprite, released from a cloven pine by Prospero.
explanation.definitionFit: Prospero's airy servant in The Tempest, freed from a split pine tree.

clue.text: Tail-to head for a denizen of this underworld

indicators.note: the instruction tells us to move one letter from the tail to the head; here the answer's tail moved to the front gives the denizen, so the S goes to the end

parts.note: a shade is a ghost, an inhabitant of the realm of the dead

explanation.surface: Move the tail to the front for a resident of this lower world.
explanation.walkthrough: The device works backwards: moving the answer's last letter S to the head gives SHADE, a ghost who lives there. So SHADE with its S moved to the end gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek realm of the dead is the classical underworld.

clue.text: A devil at cards

definitions.meaning: an old euphemism for the devil, as in 'what the ...'
the playing card bearing two pips

explanation.surface: A wizard at card games.
explanation.definitionFit: A mild oath standing for Satan, and the two in a pack of playing cards.

clue.text: The resin Zola mixed

indicators.note: mixed signals that the letters are jumbled into a new order

parts.note: Emile Zola, the French novelist

explanation.surface: The French novelist stirred up some gum.
explanation.walkthrough: Take Zola's first name, EMILE, and rearrange it.
explanation.definitionFit: A fragrant gum from tropical trees used in varnishes and ointments.

clue.text: A change to amber, certain 'to give us an opening

indicators.note: a change made to the following word rearranges its letters

parts.note: sure means certain

explanation.surface: Traffic lights turn amber, sure to let us through.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A change to' rearranges AMBER to EMBRA; add SURE. 'to give us' is link.
explanation.definitionFit: A gap in a wall or parapet through which guns fire is a splayed opening.

clue.text: Shown when a key is depressed

parts.note: D is a musical key
a piano key that is pressed down is played

explanation.surface: Something appears when a button is pushed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'depressed' looks like low spirits, but a piano key pressed down is played; so 'D is played'.
explanation.definitionFit: Exhibited, put on view, is the sense of shown.

clue.text: How to manipulate things, given the dough

definitions.text: How to manipulate things, given the dough

parts.words: How to manipulate things, given the dough
parts.note: what you do to bread mix with your hands, or what you require if you have money to make things happen

explanation.surface: Advice on pulling strings once you have the cash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dough' reads as money (slang), suggesting bribery; in the kitchen it is bread mixture worked by hand.
explanation.definitionFit: Working dough with the hands is the baker's word for massaging and pressing it.
